Pod: The smallest thing Kubernetes runs: one or more containers that share a network address and storage.
label: A key and value tag on an object, such as app: web. Other objects use labels to find it.
image: A packaged app with everything it needs to run. Kubernetes downloads it from a registry.
port: A numbered door on a network address. A web server usually listens on port 80.
Deployment: An object that keeps a set number of identical Pods running and rolls out changes to them.
replica: One copy of a Pod. Several replicas share the work and keep the app up if one fails.
selector: A rule that picks objects by their labels, such as every Pod labelled app: web.
Pod template: The part of a Deployment that describes each Pod it creates.
ReplicaSet: An object that keeps a set number of identical Pods running. Deployments manage ReplicaSets for you.
request: The CPU or memory a container needs. Kubernetes uses it to choose a node with enough room.
limit: The most CPU or memory a container may use.
namespace: A named group inside a cluster. Names only need to be unique within one namespace.
ConfigMap: An object that stores settings as text, so you can change them without rebuilding the image.
environment variable: A named value a program reads when it starts, such as DB_USER=app-user.
volume: Storage that containers in a Pod can mount as a folder.
Secret: An object for small private values, such as passwords. Stored base64-encoded, which is not encryption.
Job: An object that runs Pods until a task finishes successfully.
CronJob: An object that creates a Job on a repeating schedule, written in cron format.
key: The name before the colon on a YAML line, such as name in name: Asha.
indentation: Spaces at the start of a line. In YAML, they show which key a line belongs to.
list: Several values under one key. In YAML, each item starts with a dash and a space.
manifest: A file that describes the Kubernetes objects you want. Kubernetes works to make the cluster match it.
metadata: Details that identify an object, such as its name, namespace, and labels.
spec: The desired state: what you want Kubernetes to create or run.
status: The current state of an object, written by Kubernetes. You never write it in your file.
Service: An object that gives a group of Pods one stable name and address inside the cluster.
ClusterIP: The default Service type. Its address works only inside the cluster.
DNS: The system that turns names into network addresses. Kubernetes runs its own DNS inside the cluster.
NodePort: A Service type that opens the same port, from 30000 to 32767, on every node.
ExternalName: A Service type that makes cluster DNS answer with an outside name.
headless Service: A Service with no shared address. Looking up its name returns the address of each Pod.
DaemonSet: An object that runs one copy of a Pod on every node.
Downward API: A way for a container to read facts about its own Pod, such as its node.
LimitRange: An object that sets default and maximum sizes for each container in a namespace.
ResourceQuota: An object that caps the total CPU, memory, or objects in a namespace.
probe: A regular health check Kubernetes runs on a container, such as asking for a web page.
rollout: The process of replacing a Deployment’s Pods with new ones, a few at a time.
PodDisruptionBudget: An object that limits how many of an app’s Pods may be evicted at once.
drain: Evicting every Pod from a node, for example before an upgrade. It respects disruption budgets.
node affinity: Rules in a Pod that say which nodes it may run on, based on node labels.
Pod anti-affinity: Rules that keep a Pod away from other Pods, for example one copy per node.
topology key: A node label that groups nodes, such as by hostname or zone, for affinity rules.
taint: A mark on a node that keeps Pods off unless they tolerate it.
toleration: A setting in a Pod that lets it run on a node with a matching taint.
rolling update: Replacing a Deployment’s Pods a few at a time, so the app keeps serving.
Recreate: An update strategy that stops every old Pod before starting new ones.
blue-green: Running the new version beside the old one, then switching all traffic at once.
canary: Sending a small share of traffic to a new version before moving everyone.
HorizontalPodAutoscaler: An object that changes how many Pods run, based on measured load such as CPU.
metrics-server: A cluster add-on that collects CPU and memory use from every node.
annotation: A note on an object for tools to read. Unlike labels, annotations are not used to select objects.
load balancer: A cloud service with one outside address that spreads traffic across many machines or Pods.
Ingress: Rules that route web requests to Services by host name and path.
IngressClass: Names the controller that serves an Ingress, such as EKS Auto Mode’s Application Load Balancer.
StorageClass: A recipe that tells Kubernetes how to make storage when a claim asks for it.
PersistentVolumeClaim: A request for storage. Kubernetes finds or makes a volume to match it.
StatefulSet: Runs Pods that keep their names and their own disks when they are replaced.
Amazon EFS: An AWS file system that many machines can use at once.
access mode: How a volume may be used: by one node, by many nodes, or read-only.
NodePool: Rules for the machines EKS Auto Mode or Karpenter may launch, such as type and capacity.
ServiceAccount: An identity that Pods run as when they talk to Kubernetes or, through Pod Identity, to AWS.
Pod Identity: An EKS feature that gives Pods temporary AWS keys from an IAM role linked to their ServiceAccount.
